title: Agony Point, Batasia and the toy train's loops
meta_description: Why the Darjeeling toy train climbs in loops and zigzags: Agony Point, the Batasia Loop, the reverses near Tindharia, and where to watch them.
summary: The toy train climbs from the plains to 2,258 m at Ghum on two-foot track, and it cannot do that in a straight line. Loops let it gain height by circling over itself; zigzag reverses let it climb a slope by going forward, then backward. Agony Point and the Batasia Loop are the two most famous.
key_takeaways: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway uses loops and zigzag reverses because a train on steel rails cannot climb a mountainside as steeply as a road can.
Agony Point, near Tindharia on the lower line, is the tightest loop on the railway, and the train almost touches its own tail as it turns.
The Batasia Loop below Ghum was added in 1919 to ease the climb out of Darjeeling, and today it is the photo stop on every joyride.
The joyride from Darjeeling shows you Batasia; to see Agony Point and the reverses you need the full line or a road trip toward Tindharia.

sections.heading: A railway that had to follow a road
paras: Before 1881 everything that went up to Darjeeling, from tea chests to newly posted officers, went by the Hill Cart Road: bullock carts, ponies, porters and palanquins on a long climb from the plains. Franklin Prestage, an agent of the Eastern Bengal Railway, proposed a steam tramway that would run along that same road. The company he helped found, the Darjeeling Steam Tramway Company, soon renamed the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, began work in 1879 and reached Darjeeling in July 1881.

The key decision was the gauge. The rails were laid only 610 mm apart, two feet, which allowed curves far tighter than a normal railway could take. That let the line hug the hillside and cross the road again and again, as it still does in Kurseong and Ghum bazaars. But a narrow gauge does not solve the other problem: gradient. Steel wheels on steel rails lose grip on a steep slope, and the climb from Siliguri, at about 120 m, to Ghum, at 2,258 m, is relentless. Somewhere the engineers had to buy extra distance, and they bought it with loops and zigzags.

sections.heading: Loops and zigzags, in plain words
paras: A loop is a spiral. The track climbs steadily round a hill or a knoll, turns a full circle and passes over or beside its own earlier line, now several metres higher. The train never stops; it simply runs further to gain the same height, which keeps the gradient gentle enough for the engine to grip.

A zigzag, which railway people here call a reverse, works differently. Where the slope is too steep and too narrow for a loop, the line runs forward up one leg to a dead end, a staff member changes the points, and the train backs up the next leg, then runs forward again on the third. Watching it from inside is strange at first: the scenery you just passed comes back into view from above. The reverses mostly sit on the lower part of the line, between Rangtong and Tindharia, where the hills rise most sharply from the plains.

Neither trick is unique to Darjeeling, but few railways use so many of them on one line. The layout has also changed over the years. Some loops and reverses were added after the first years of running, and storms and landslides, including damage in the monsoon floods of the 1990s, led to sections being realigned. Counts quoted in older books and on signboards do not always agree, so we have not given one here.

sections.heading: Agony Point, the tightest turn
paras: Agony Point is a loop near Tindharia, on the stretch where the line climbs out of the foothills toward Kurseong. Its fame comes from its radius. The curve is so tight that the engine and the last carriage seem to face each other as the train comes round, and people standing on the outside of the bend can watch the whole train wrap around the knoll. Older photographs show a signboard there with the name painted on it.

Nobody seems to know for certain who named it or why. The usual explanation is the obvious one: the agony of the engine labouring round the curve, or of passengers who felt the carriages lean. We have not found a reliable source that settles it, so treat any confident story about the name as a guess.

Tindharia is also where the railway's main workshop has stood since the early years, repairing and rebuilding the small locomotives. The B-class steam engines, built in Britain from 1889 onward, still pull the steam joyrides from Darjeeling, and some of their maintenance work is done here. If you are travelling by road, the Hill Cart Road runs close to the line around Tindharia and you can see track, workshop sheds and, with luck, a passing train.

sections.heading: Batasia, the loop everyone photographs
paras: The Batasia Loop sits about 5 km from Darjeeling, on the descent from Ghum. The line from Ghum to Darjeeling actually runs downhill, because Ghum is higher than the town, and the gradient on that last stretch was hard work for trains climbing back out. In 1919 the railway built the loop to ease it: the track now spirals round a knoll, passing over itself, and loses height more gently. The name is usually explained as coming from the Nepali word for wind, batas, for a ridge that is often breezy.

The middle of the loop is now a landscaped garden with the Gorkha War Memorial, raised in honour of Gorkha soldiers of the Indian Army who died in action since independence. On a clear morning from October to early December, or in March and April, Kanchenjunga stands behind it across the valley. Entry to the garden is a small fee, around ₹20–50 for Indians, and stalls around the edge sell woollens and tea.

Every joyride from Darjeeling stops at Batasia for about 10 minutes. If you would rather watch the train than ride it, walk up from the town or take a shared vehicle toward Ghum, pay at the gate and wait for a joyride to circle below you.

sections.heading: Ghum, the top of the line
paras: Ghum station, at 2,258 m, is the highest point on the railway and one of the highest stations in India. From here the line drops about 200 m into Darjeeling over a few kilometres. Joyrides wait at Ghum for roughly half an hour, which is long enough to walk round the small railway museum on the platform, with old tickets, lamps, photographs and a vintage engine.

Ghoom Monastery, Yiga Choeling, built in 1850 and known for its large Maitreya Buddha, is a short walk below the station. If you take the joyride in the morning and get off at Ghum to see the monastery, you can return to Darjeeling by shared jeep for ₹30–50 a seat instead of waiting for the train.

sections.heading: Seeing the loops for yourself
paras: For most visitors the realistic option is a joyride: about two hours return from Darjeeling to Ghum, with stops at Batasia and Ghum. The steam joyride costs roughly ₹1,500–1,800 a seat and the diesel one ₹1,000–1,300, both booked on IRCTC. Seats sell out in October, the Puja holidays, late December and May–June.

To see Agony Point and the reverses from the train, you need the full line between NJP and Darjeeling, which takes seven to eight hours or more and has often been suspended for months after landslides on the lower section. When it runs, sit facing forward and watch the stretch above Rangtong. The other way is by road: if you hire a car from Siliguri, ask the driver to take the Hill Cart Road through Tindharia rather than the faster Rohini road, and stop where the track crosses. Toy train services, timetables and fares change often, so check current status before you travel.
list: Book joyrides early in your stay, so a cancellation leaves you time to retry.
Morning departures give the best chance of a clear view at Batasia.
On the full line, carry water and snacks; station stops are irregular.
Respect the track: the train runs right past shop fronts and people on foot.

faqs.q: Does the Darjeeling joyride pass Agony Point?
faqs.a: No. The joyride runs only between Darjeeling and Ghum, so it covers the Batasia Loop but not Agony Point, which is near Tindharia on the lower line. To pass Agony Point by train you need the full NJP to Darjeeling service, when it is running, or a section that includes Tindharia. You can also see the area from the Hill Cart Road by car. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why does the toy train go backwards at some points?
faqs.a: Those are the zigzag reverses. Where the hillside is too steep and narrow for a loop, the line climbs in short legs: forward to a dead end, points changed, then backward up the next leg, then forward again. It lets the train gain height on a slope it could not climb directly. Most reverses are on the lower line between Rangtong and Tindharia, so you see them only on the full line.

faqs.q: When was the Batasia Loop built?
faqs.a: The Batasia Loop was built in 1919, nearly 40 years after the railway reached Darjeeling in 1881. It eased the gradient between Ghum and Darjeeling by letting the track spiral round a knoll and pass over itself. The centre is now a garden with the Gorkha War Memorial, and every joyride stops there for about 10 minutes for photographs.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to see the Batasia Loop?
faqs.a: Entry to the Batasia Loop garden is a small fee, roughly ₹20–50 for Indian visitors, collected at the gate. You can walk or take a shared vehicle there from Darjeeling, about 5 km. If you go by joyride, the stop is included in the ticket, which is roughly ₹1,500–1,800 for steam and ₹1,000–1,300 for diesel. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the full toy train line from NJP to Darjeeling running?
faqs.a: It varies. The full line has been suspended or run only in sections for long periods after landslides, especially between Tindharia and Kurseong, and has mostly used diesel engines in recent years. The Darjeeling to Ghum joyrides are far more reliable. Look up the NJP to DJ train on IRCTC close to your dates and check current status before you travel, keeping a road plan in reserve.
